newsitem.title: SPAIN: Potential pressures glimpsed for Spanish inflation.
newsitem.headline: Potential pressures glimpsed for Spanish inflation.

text.p: Spanish inflation, which edged up to 1.6 percent in June, may be starting to show the influence of strong economic growth and potential price pressure, economists said on Friday.
Most are now looking to the 1998 budget for a tighter fiscal policy, curbing the impact of expected price pressures next year and facilitating a fresh interestrate cut later this year.
But no rate cuts are likely for the moment.

"Caution on the part of the monetary authority is based on core inflation's resistance to a further fall, which reflects the behaviour of prices both in services and manufacturing," a research note from Central Hispano bank said.

"This risk could increase in the coming months in a climate of accelerating consumption and economic growth...A 1998 budget which reflects a clearly anti-cyclical fiscal policy would reduce these risks and pave the way for the necessary convergence in official rates with those in Germany."

The June Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 1.6 percent year-on-year, a notch up from May's 1.5 percent historic low. Core inflation, which excludes energy and fresh food, rose 0.2 percent from May for an unchanged 1.9 percent year-on-year rate.
The figures showed improvement in comparison with this time last year, when prices were fuelled by factors such as the knock-on effects of the "mad cow" crisis in the beef industry.

Some see the price index ticking up in the second half of this year, but not substantially, with the consensus forecast below the government's official 2.2 percent for end-1997. But many economists focused on stubborn services prices, which gained 0.3 percent from May for a rise of 3.2 percent year-on-year, as a potential danger.

"Prices for services are stuck at rates around three percent. The situation in services hasn't changed...It is the most worrying component, although the CPI below two percent isn't alarming," said Fernando Gutierrez, chief economist at Argentaria in Madrid.
There may also be warning signals in tourism and property prices, Banco Bilba Vizcaya (BBV) said.

"The recovery in economic activity could be applying pressure, with an added agravation in the case of housing in that it is a sector in which there are still strong restrictions regarding land," a BBV research note said.

Overall, economists saw the Bank of Spain's potential to move on key money rates as limited. The central bank has to find the delicate balance between allowing strong economic growth to continue without price pressures filtering through longer term, they said.

"Growth is very strong and we expect (gross domestic product) to average around three percent this year. This doesn't put upside pressure on prices this year because there's an unusually long lag in the impact. We see risks for (inflation) in the second half of 1998, with the CPI possibly ending at 2.5-3.0 percent." said Jose Luis Alzola at Salomon Brothers in London.

Analysts agree that the prospect of Spain's entry into monetary union in 1999 will prompt the central bank to gradually cut official interest rates, bringing them nearer to Germany's. They say this is the only way they can rule out an excessive appreciation of the peseta against the mark ahead of the launch of the euro.
